# Reversibility and Non-Flow Processes {#sec-ch3}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Demonstrate the concept of **quasi-equilibrium** and **reversibility** in
  thermodynamics.
- Define and use **specific heat capacities** in thermodynamic problems.
- Analyse different **polytropic processes** (isochoric, isobaric, etc.).
:::

*Non-flow* processes are processes of a **closed system**: energy (heat and
work) crosses the boundary, but mass does not.

## Reversibility

In the last chapter, the energy equation for a process was presented in the
form of:

![](figures/img/ch3-system.png){width=26%}

$$
q + w = u_2 - u_1
$$

As mentioned earlier, in general, the amount of work and heat depends on the
process, and therefore they cannot be expressed as a function of system
properties, $f(T, P, \ldots)$. This can be, however, done for certain ideal
processes called *quasi-equilibrium* processes (*quasi* means *almost*).

### Quasi-equilibrium process

A process during which the system only deviates from thermodynamic equilibrium
by an infinitesimal amount. In other words, the system is passed through a
continuous series of equilibrium states.

![](figures/out/ch3-quasi-path.svg){width=86%}

::: {.note}
During a quasi-equilibrium process, intensive properties (e.g. $T$, $P$) of a
system are uniform throughout the whole system.
:::

::: {.note}
Quasi-equilibrium processes are ***reversible***. This means that **both** the
system **and** the surroundings can be returned to their exact initial
conditions.
:::

### Work and reversibility

In a quasi-equilibrium (reversible) expansion/compression, the external
pressure is infinitesimally different from the system pressure.

![](figures/img/ch3-piston-masses.png){width=24%}

Incremental masses are removed one at a time during the expansion.
$P_\text{ext}$ acts on the piston from above; $P$ is the pressure of the gas.

![](figures/out/ch3-rev-steps.svg){width=58%}

Each small mass removed lowers $P_\text{ext}$ a little and the gas expands
until its pressure $P$ matches it again, so $P \approx P_\text{ext}$ at every
step of the process.

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Start from the CH2 work integral; in a reversible process $P_\text{ext} \approx P$."}
$$
W = -\int P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}V
\qquad \xrightarrow{\ P_\text{ext}\,\approx\,P\ } \qquad
W_\text{rev} = -\int P\,\mathrm{d}V
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
W_\text{rev} = -\int P\,\mathrm{d}V
$$ {#eq-ch3-wrev}
:::

::: {.note}
Quasi-equilibrium processes are **very slow** and may never happen in reality,
but many actual processes approach a quasi-equilibrium process.
:::

**Irreversible work.** **Free expansion** is the classical example of a process
that is NOT quasi-equilibrium. A gas at $P_1, V_1$ is held on one side of a
partition, with a vacuum ($P = 0$) on the other. The partition is removed and
the gas fills the whole container, reaching $P_2, V_2$.

![](figures/out/ch3-free-expansion.svg){width=100%}

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="What pushes back on the gas? Nothing: $P_\text{ext} = 0$, so $W = 0$."}
Nothing pushes back on the expanding gas, $P_\text{ext} = 0$, so
$$
W = -\int \underbrace{P_\text{ext}}_{=\,0}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0
$$
:::

Free expansion is NOT quasi-equilibrium, and therefore it is
**irreversible**.

::: {.note}
Irreversible processes are usually shown by dashed lines in $PV$ diagrams.
:::

::: {.note}
Free expansion is an extreme case. In reality, expansion processes are
something between free expansion and a quasi-equilibrium (reversible)
expansion.
:::

![](figures/out/ch3-exp-comp.svg){width=74%}

**Magnitude of expansion work done by the system:**

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Expansion: the gas pushes the piston out, so $P \ge P_\text{ext}$; compare the two integrals."}
To push the piston out, $P \ge P_\text{ext}$, so
$$
|W| = \int P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}V \;\le\; \int P\,\mathrm{d}V
$$
:::

**Magnitude of compression work done on the system:**

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Compression: the surroundings push the piston in, so $P \le P_\text{ext}$."}
To push the piston in, $P \le P_\text{ext}$, so
$$
|W| = \int P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}V \;\ge\; \int P\,\mathrm{d}V
$$
:::

::: {.key}
The ideal (reversible) process, with $|W| = \int P\,\mathrm{d}V$, gives the
**maximum expansion work** done by the system and needs the **minimum
compression work** done on the system.
:::

### Heat and reversibility

The part of the surroundings that exchanges heat with the system is called a
**heat reservoir**. We assume that heat exchange cannot change the temperature
of a heat reservoir, owing to its very large heat capacity. A heat reservoir
can be either a **heat source** ($T_\text{H.R.} > T_\text{sys}$) or a **heat
sink** ($T_\text{H.R.} < T_\text{sys}$).

![The sea, the atmosphere and a fire: examples of heat reservoirs.](figures/img/ch3-reservoirs.png){width=88%}

The heat transfer between the system and a heat reservoir can be done either
***reversibly*** or ***irreversibly***.

::: {.example}
Imagine we want to raise the system temperature from 100 °C to 200 °C. Compare
the two ways of doing it shown below: putting the system straight into a heat
source at 200 °C (left), or heating it with a heat source that is always only
$\mathrm{d}T$ hotter than the system (right). Which one is reversible?

![](figures/img/ch3-heat-sources.png){width=62%}

**Step 1.** *System at 100 °C inside a source at 200 °C: sketch how the
temperature varies across a section A–A of the system while it heats up. Is it
uniform?*

::: {.gap height="50mm" hint="Temperature profile across A--A: 200 at the walls, 100 inside at first; the profiles evolve, never uniform. Non-quasi $\Rightarrow$ irreversible."}
![](figures/out/ch3-temp-profile.svg){width=62%}

The part of the system next to the wall heats up first, so while the system
heats up its temperature is **not uniform**. The process is not
quasi-equilibrium:
$$
\text{non-quasi-equilibrium} \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{irreversible}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Now the source is only $\mathrm{d}T$ hotter than the system, at
every instant. What happens to the temperature inside the system?*

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Source at $T + \mathrm{d}T$: $T$ stays uniform, the system passes through equilibrium states. Quasi-eq. $\Rightarrow$ reversible."}
The heat flows across an infinitesimal temperature difference, so the
temperature of the system stays uniform and it passes through a continuous
series of equilibrium states:
$$
\text{quasi-equilibrium} \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{reversible}
$$
:::
:::

### Energy equation in differential form

For a *reversible* process, the energy equation can be written in a
differential form.

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Write $Q + W = \Delta U$ for an infinitesimal step: $\delta Q + \delta W = \mathrm{d}U$."}
$$
Q + W = \Delta U
\qquad \longrightarrow \qquad
\underbrace{\delta Q}_{\text{inexact}} + \underbrace{\delta W}_{\text{inexact}}
= \underbrace{\mathrm{d}U}_{\text{exact}}
$$
:::

$U$ is a property, so $\int_1^2 \mathrm{d}U = U_2 - U_1$. Work and heat are
not, so $\int_1^2 \delta W \neq W_2 - W_1$: there is no such thing as "$W_2$"
or "$W_1$".

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Reversibility: $\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$ (the system pressure, not $P_\text{ext}$)."}
For a reversible process, @eq-ch3-wrev gives $\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$, with
the **system** pressure $P$ in place of $P_\text{ext}$:
$$
\delta Q - P\,\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}U
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\delta Q - P\,\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}U
$$ {#eq-ch3-diff}

the differential form of the energy equation, for a **reversible** process.
:::

::: {.note}
$\delta q$ and $\delta w$, as *inexact* differentials, are specific types of
differentials used in thermodynamics to express the **path dependence**. The
integral of an inexact differential cannot be identified only by knowing the
initial and final states. This is in contrast with the concept of the *exact*
differential (e.g. $\mathrm{d}u$, $\mathrm{d}T$ and $\mathrm{d}P$), which is
path independent.
:::

## Constant volume (isochoric) process

The First Law for a *reversible* constant-volume process can be written as:

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$\mathrm{d}V = 0$ kills the work term; divide by the mass. Label it (I)."}
$\mathrm{d}V = 0$, so
$$
\delta Q - P\underbrace{\mathrm{d}V}_{=\,0} = \mathrm{d}U
\;\;\rightarrow\;\;
\delta Q_v = \mathrm{d}U_v
\;\;\xrightarrow{\ \div\,\text{mass}\ }\;\;
\delta q_v = \mathrm{d}u_v \tag{I}
$$
:::

**Heat capacity** $C$ is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a
substance by 1 °C. The SI unit of heat capacity is [J/K]:

$$
\delta Q = C\,\mathrm{d}T \qquad \left[\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{K}}\right]
$$

**Specific heat capacity** $c$ is the heat capacity of a substance divided by
its mass, with the SI unit of [J/(kg K)]:

$$
c = \frac{C}{m}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\delta Q}_{[\mathrm{J}]}
= \underbrace{m}_{[\mathrm{kg}]}\,c\,\underbrace{\mathrm{d}T}_{[\mathrm{K}]},
\quad c\;\left[\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}\right]
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\delta q = c\,\mathrm{d}T
$$

**Specific heat capacity at constant volume, $c_v$:** the specific heat capacity
$c$ for a constant-volume process:

$$
\delta q_v = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T \tag{II}
$$

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Combine (I) and (II)."}
Combining (I) and (II):
$$
\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T \qquad (\text{at constant } v)
$$
:::

$c_v$ can therefore be defined as a system (thermodynamic) property:

::: {.key}
$$
c_v = \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}T}\right)_v
$$ {#eq-ch3-cv}
:::

## Constant pressure (isobaric) process

The energy equation (i.e. the First Law) for a *reversible* constant-pressure
process can be written as:

$$
\delta q - P\,\mathrm{d}v = \mathrm{d}u
$$

::: {.note}
*Reminder:* product rule, $\mathrm{d}(fg) = g\,\mathrm{d}f + f\,\mathrm{d}g$.
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Move $P\,\mathrm{d}v$ across and add $v\,\mathrm{d}P$, which is zero at constant $P$."}
$$
\delta q = \mathrm{d}u + \underbrace{P\,\mathrm{d}v + v\underbrace{\mathrm{d}P}_{=\,0}}_{\mathrm{d}(Pv)}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="So $\delta q = \mathrm{d}(u + Pv)$; call $u + Pv = h$."}
$$
\delta q = \mathrm{d}(\underbrace{u + Pv}_{h})
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\delta q_P = \mathrm{d}h_P
$$
:::

$h$ is the specific **enthalpy**:

::: {.key}
$$
H = U + PV \;\;[\mathrm{J}], \qquad h = u + Pv \;\;\left[\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}\right],
\qquad H = m h
$$ {#eq-ch3-h}
:::

::: {.note}
Enthalpy (*EN-thal-pee*) is a system property, so its change from one state to
another does not depend on the process. $H$ is an extensive property, and the
specific enthalpy $h = H/m$ is its intensive counterpart.
:::

::: {.note}
Enthalpy is always greater than internal energy.
:::

**Specific heat capacity at constant pressure, $c_P$:** the specific heat
capacity $c$ for a constant-pressure process:

$$
\delta q_P = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T
$$

Similar to $c_v$, $c_P$ can be defined as a system property.

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="The energy equation gave $\delta q_P = \mathrm{d}h_P$; compare with $\delta q_P = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T$."}
The energy equation gave $\delta q_P = \mathrm{d}h_P$, and by definition
$\delta q_P = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, so $\mathrm{d}h = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ at
constant $P$.
:::

::: {.key}
$$
c_P = \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}T}\right)_P
$$ {#eq-ch3-cp}
:::

::: {.note}
In general, two independent system properties are enough to identify $c_v$ or
$c_P$ (like any other system property).
:::

## Specific heat capacities for ideal gases

One of the important features of an ***ideal gas*** is that its **internal
energy only depends on its temperature**: $u = u(T)$.

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$u$ depends on $T$ only, so the 'at constant $v$' can be dropped."}
$u$ depends on $T$ alone, so the constraint "at constant $v$" in @eq-ch3-cv
can be dropped:
$$
c_v = \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}T}\right)_{v}
\;\xrightarrow{\ u\,=\,u(T)\ }\;
c_v = \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}T}
\;\rightarrow\;
\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T
$$
:::

From the ideal-gas equation, $Pv = RT$. Thus:

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$h = u(T) + RT$: a function of $T$ only."}
$$
h = u + Pv = u(T) + RT
\quad\rightarrow\quad
h = h(T) \quad \text{(ideal gas)}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Same argument for $c_P$: drop the 'at constant $P$'."}
$$
c_P = \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}T}\right)_{P}
\;\xrightarrow{\ h\,=\,h(T)\ }\;
c_P = \frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}T}
\;\rightarrow\;
\mathrm{d}h = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T
$$
:::

::: {.key}
For an **ideal gas**, going through **any process**:
$$
\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T, \qquad \mathrm{d}h = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T
$$ {#eq-ch3-dudh}
:::

Therefore, for an ideal gas, $c_v$ and $c_P$ only depend on $T$:
$c_v = c_v(T)$, $c_P = c_P(T)$.

Over small temperature changes, it is often assumed that $c_v$ and $c_P$ are
**constant for ideal gases**.

::: {.note}
$\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$ and $\mathrm{d}h = c_P\,\mathrm{d}T$ are valid
for ideal gases going through **any process**, not only constant pressure or
constant volume.
:::

We can also relate the specific heat capacities of an ideal gas to its gas
constant $R$ as follows:

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Differentiate $h = u + Pv$; each term: $c_P\,\mathrm{d}T$, $c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$, $R\,\mathrm{d}T$ (from $Pv = RT$)."}
$$
h = u + Pv
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\mathrm{d}h}_{c_P\,\mathrm{d}T}
= \underbrace{\mathrm{d}u}_{c_v\,\mathrm{d}T}
+ \underbrace{\mathrm{d}(Pv)}_{R\,\mathrm{d}T}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Cancel $\mathrm{d}T$."}
$$
c_P\,\mathrm{d}T = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T + R\,\mathrm{d}T
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
c_P = c_v + R
$$ {#eq-ch3-cpcv}
:::

::: {.example}
Calculate the change of enthalpy as 2 kg of a gas is heated from 300 K to
500 K. Assume ideal gas behaviour for the gas, with $R = 200~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$
and $c_v = 800~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.

**Step 1.** *For an ideal gas, how is a change of enthalpy related to a change
of temperature? Which specific heat do you need?*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$\Delta H = m\,\Delta h = m c_P \Delta T$: we need $c_P$, not $c_v$."}
$$
\Delta H = m\,\Delta h = m\,c_P\,\Delta T \tag{$*$}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *You are given $c_v$, not $c_P$. How are they related for an ideal
gas?*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$c_P = c_v + R = 800 + 200 = 1000$ J/(kg K)."}
$$
c_P = c_v + R = 800~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} + 200~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
= 1000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
$$
:::

**Step 3.** *Substitute into ($*$).*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$2 \times 1000 \times 200 = 4\times10^5$ J $= 400$ kJ."}
$$
\Delta H = 2~\mathrm{kg} \times 1000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \times 200~\mathrm{K}
= \boxed{4\times10^{5}~\mathrm{J} = 400~\mathrm{kJ}}
$$
:::
:::

An expression that will appear often is the **ratio of specific heats**
$\gamma$, defined as $c_P/c_v$:

::: {.key}
$$
\gamma = \frac{c_P}{c_v} > 1
$$

since $c_P - c_v = R > 0$, so $c_P > c_v$.
:::

| | $c_v$ | $c_P$ | $\gamma = c_P/c_v$ |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Monatomic (He, Ne) | $3R/2$ | $5R/2$ | $5/3$ |
| Diatomic (O$_2$, N$_2$) | $5R/2$ | $7R/2$ | $7/5$ |

: Specific heats of ideal gases.

## Isothermal process

An isothermal process is a change of a system in which the **system temperature
remains constant**.

::: {.note}
Heat is NOT necessarily zero in an isothermal process: heat can be exchanged
(reversibly) with a reservoir at $T + \mathrm{d}T$ while the system stays at
$T_\text{sys}$.
:::

$$
\delta q - P\,\mathrm{d}v = \mathrm{d}u
$$

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Ideal gas: $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T = 0$ at constant $T$."}
For an ideal gas, $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T = 0$ since $T$ is constant:
$$
\delta q_T = P\,\mathrm{d}v
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$Pv = RT$ with $RT$ constant: $P \propto 1/v$, like $y \sim 1/x$."}
For an ideal gas,
$$
Pv = RT \;\rightarrow\; P = \frac{\overbrace{RT}^{\text{constant}}}{v}
\qquad\text{i.e. } P \propto \frac{1}{v}\;\;(\text{like } y \sim 1/x)
$$
:::

::: {.key}
Isothermal process of an ideal gas:
$$
Pv = \text{const}, \qquad \delta q_T = P\,\mathrm{d}v
$$
:::

![Isotherms of an ideal gas in the $P$–$v$ diagram.](figures/out/ch3-isotherms.svg){width=56%}

## Adiabatic process

A process in which there is no heat transfer ($Q = 0$) is called an
***adiabatic*** (*ay-dye-uh-BAT-ik*) process. This can usually be accomplished
by:

![Insulation (left), or a rapid process, e.g. the compression in an engine cylinder (right).](figures/img/ch3-adiabatic.png){width=56%}

According to the energy equation (assuming a reversible process), for an ideal
gas ($Pv = RT$, $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$):

$$
\delta q - P\,\mathrm{d}v = \mathrm{d}u
$$

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$\delta q = 0$ and $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$."}
$\delta q = 0$ and $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$:
$$
-P\,\mathrm{d}v = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Replace $P$ by $RT/v$."}
With $P = RT/v$:
$$
-\frac{RT}{v}\,\mathrm{d}v = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="22mm" hint="Separate variables and integrate; $\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \mathrm{d}x/x = \ln(x_2/x_1)$."}
Separating the variables and integrating, with
$\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x} = \ln\frac{x_2}{x_1}$:
$$
-R\int_{v_1}^{v_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v} = c_v\int_{T_1}^{T_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
-R\ln\!\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right) = c_v\ln\!\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Move the coefficients into the logarithms as powers."}
Moving the coefficients into the logarithms as powers:
$$
\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^{-R} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{c_v}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="24mm" hint="Eliminate $T$: $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)(v_2/v_1)$; then use $\gamma = c_P/c_v = (R + c_v)/c_v$."}
From $Pv = RT$, $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)\left(\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}\right)$, so
$$
\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^{-(R + c_v)} = \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{c_v}
\quad\xrightarrow{\ \gamma\,=\,\frac{c_P}{c_v}\,=\,\frac{R + c_v}{c_v}\ }\quad
\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^{\gamma}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
P_1 v_1^{\gamma} = P_2 v_2^{\gamma}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
Reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas:
$$
P v^{\gamma} = \text{Constant}
$$ {#eq-ch3-adiabatic}
:::

## Polytropic process

All of the processes discussed earlier can be generally expressed as a
**polytropic process**, given by:

$$
P v^{n} = \text{const.}
$$

The *polytropic exponent* $n$ is indicative of the type of process, and it can
vary from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$.

::: {.gap height="10mm" hint="Isobaric: $P = \text{const}$ means $Pv^0 = \text{const}$, so $n = 0$."}
**Isobaric:** $P v^{n} = \text{const}$ with $P = \text{const}$ $\rightarrow$ $n = 0$.
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Isochoric: take the $n$-th root, $P^{1/n}v = \text{const}$; let $n \to \infty$."}
**Isochoric:** take the $n$-th root of both sides,
$$
\sqrt[n]{P v^{n}} = \sqrt[n]{\text{const}}
\;\rightarrow\;
P^{1/n}\,v = \text{const}^{*}
\qquad n \to \infty \;\Rightarrow\; v = \text{const}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Isothermal (ideal gas): $Pv = \text{const}$, so $n = 1$."}
**Isothermal** (ideal gas): $P v^{n} = \text{const}$ and $P v = \text{const}$
$\rightarrow$ $n = 1$.
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Adiabatic (ideal gas): $Pv^\gamma = \text{const}$, so $n = \gamma = c_P/c_v$."}
**Adiabatic** (ideal gas): $P v^{\gamma} = \text{const}$ $\rightarrow$
$n = \gamma = c_P/c_v$.
:::

| | Polytropic | $Pv^{n} = \text{const}$ | $n$ | Work [J/kg] |
|:-:|:--|:--|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | **Isobaric** | $P = \text{const}$ | $0$ | $-P\,(v_2 - v_1)$ |
| 2 | **Isochoric** | $v = \text{const}$ | $\infty$ | $0$ |
| 3 | **Isothermal** | $Pv = \text{const}$ (only for ideal gas) | $1$ | $-Pv\ln\left(v_2/v_1\right)$ |
| 4 | **Adiabatic** | $Pv^{\gamma} = \text{const}$ (only for ideal gas) | $\gamma > 1$ | $\dfrac{P_2 v_2 - P_1 v_1}{\gamma - 1}$ |

: The polytropic family of processes. In general, $w = \dfrac{P_2 v_2 - P_1 v_1}{n - 1}$ for $n \neq 1$.

![Polytropic expansions from the same initial state. The dotted lines are isotherms, $T_1 > T_2 > T_3$.](figures/out/ch3-polytropic-paths.svg){width=70%}

Let us derive a relationship for the amount of **work** in a ***reversible
polytropic*** process, $Pv^{n} = \text{const}$:

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Reversible: $P_\text{ext} = P$; then $P = \text{const}/v^n$ comes out of the integral."}
$$
w = -\int P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}v
\;\xrightarrow{\ P_\text{ext}\,=\,P\ }\;
w = -\int P\,\mathrm{d}v = -\text{Const.}\int_{v_1}^{v_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v^{n}}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="$\int \mathrm{d}x/x^n = x^{1-n}/(1-n)$ for $n \neq 1$."}
With $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^{n}}
= \left.\frac{x^{1-n}}{1-n}\right|_{x_1}^{x_2}$ for $n \neq 1$:
$$
w = -P v^{n}\,\frac{v_2^{\,1-n} - v_1^{\,1-n}}{1 - n}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="The constant $Pv^n$ equals $P_1v_1^n$ and also $P_2v_2^n$: use each with its own term."}
The constant $Pv^{n}$ equals both $P_1 v_1^{n}$ and $P_2 v_2^{n}$; use each one
with its own term:
$$
w = -\frac{P_2 v_2^{n}\,v_2^{\,1-n} - P_1 v_1^{n}\,v_1^{\,1-n}}{1 - n}
  = \frac{P_2 v_2 - P_1 v_1}{n - 1}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
w = \frac{P_2 v_2 - P_1 v_1}{n - 1} \qquad (n \neq 1)
$$ {#eq-ch3-wpoly}
:::

For $n = 1$ the formula above breaks down (division by zero).

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="$n = 1$ is the isothermal process: $P_1v_1 = P_2v_2 = Pv$; now $\int \mathrm{d}x/x = \ln(x_2/x_1)$."}
$n = 1$ is the **isothermal** process (for an ideal gas), $P_1 v_1 = P_2 v_2 = Pv$,
and with $\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x} = \ln\frac{x_2}{x_1}$:
$$
w = -Pv\int_{v_1}^{v_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v} = -Pv\ln\!\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
w = -Pv\ln\!\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right) \qquad (n = 1)
$$ {#eq-ch3-wiso}
:::

::: {.example}
A gas in a piston–cylinder assembly undergoes a reversible polytropic process.
The initial pressure is 3 bar, the initial volume is $0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$, and the
final volume is $0.2~\mathrm{m^3}$. Determine the work for the process, in kJ,
if (a) $n = 1.5$, (b) $n = 1$, and (c) $n = 0$.

![](figures/img/ch3-polytropic-piston.png){width=40%}

**Step 1.** *(a) @eq-ch3-wpoly needs $P_2$. Find it from $PV^{n} = \text{const}$.*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$P_2 = P_1(V_1/V_2)^n = 3 \times 0.5^{1.5} = 1.061$ bar."}
$$
P_1V_1^{n} = P_2V_2^{n}
\;\Rightarrow\;
P_2 = P_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{n}
= 3~\text{bar}\times\left(\frac{0.1}{0.2}\right)^{1.5} = 1.061~\text{bar}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *(a) Multiply @eq-ch3-wpoly by the mass to get the total work, and
substitute in SI units.*

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="$W = (P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)/(n-1) = (21.21 - 30)/0.5 = -17.6$ kJ."}
$$
W = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{n - 1}
= \frac{1.061\times10^{5}\times0.2 - 3\times10^{5}\times0.1}{1.5 - 1}~\mathrm{J}
= \boxed{-17.6~\mathrm{kJ}}
$$
:::

**Step 3.** *(b) $n = 1$: which formula applies now?*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$W = -P_1V_1\ln(V_2/V_1) = -3\times10^4 \ln 2 = -20.8$ kJ."}
$$
W = -P_1V_1\ln\!\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
= -3\times10^{5}\times0.1\times\ln\!\left(\frac{0.2}{0.1}\right)~\mathrm{J}
= \boxed{-20.8~\mathrm{kJ}}
$$
:::

**Step 4.** *(c) $n = 0$: what kind of process is this?*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$n = 0$ is isobaric: $W = -P(V_2 - V_1) = -30$ kJ."}
$n = 0$ is a constant-pressure process:
$$
W = -P\left(V_2 - V_1\right) = -3\times10^{5}\times\left(0.2 - 0.1\right)~\mathrm{J}
= \boxed{-30~\mathrm{kJ}}
$$
:::

**Step 5.** *All three are expansions between the same two volumes. Why do the
magnitudes differ?*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="All negative (expansion). The smaller $n$, the higher the pressure stays, so the larger the area under the path."}
All three are negative, as expected for an expansion. The smaller $n$ is, the
more slowly the pressure falls as the gas expands, so the larger the area under
the path in the $P$–$V$ diagram: $|W_{n=0}| > |W_{n=1}| > |W_{n=1.5}|$.
:::
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

## End-of-chapter problems {#sec-ch3-problems}

::: {.tryfirst}
Have a real go at every problem here before you look at a solution. Worked
solutions are released after the lectures, but reading a solution is not the
same as being able to produce one: the time you spend stuck on a problem is
where most of the learning happens. Only once you have an answer of your own,
or have tried every approach you can think of, check it against the solution,
and compare the method, not just the final number.
:::

**P3.1 [easy].** Air is heated from 300 to 350 K at constant volume. Find the
heat transfer per unit mass in kJ/kg. (Assume ideal gas and
$c_v = 0.72~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 8 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 24 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 48 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 36

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
For a constant-volume process:
$$
q_v = c_v\,\Delta T = 0.72~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \times 50~\mathrm{K}
= \boxed{36~\mathrm{kJ/kg}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
:::
:::

**P3.2 [easy].** In the previous question (P3.1), find the heat transfer per
unit mass in kJ/kg if the process is constant pressure (isobaric).
($R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$)

**(a)** 100.6 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 50.35 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 20.9 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 10

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
For a constant-pressure process, $q_P = c_P\,\Delta T$, and for an ideal gas
$c_P = c_v + R$:
$$
q_P = c_P\,\Delta T = \left(c_v + R\right)\Delta T
= \left(0.72 + 0.287\right)\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \times 50~\mathrm{K}
= \boxed{50.35~\mathrm{kJ/kg}} \quad \text{(b)}
$$

For a given $\Delta T$, $q_P > q_v$ because $c_P > c_v$.
:::
:::

**P3.3 [easy].** A rigid container has 2 kg of nitrogen gas at 100 kPa, 1200 K
that is heated to 1400 K. Find the heat transfer in kJ.
($c_v = 0.745~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$)

![](figures/img/ch3-p-rigid-tank.png){width=36%}

**(a)** 298 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 150 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 138 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 369

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Since the container is **rigid**, the volume does not change during the
process:
$$
Q = m\,c_v\,\Delta T
= 2~\mathrm{kg} \times 0.745~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \times 200~\mathrm{K}
= \boxed{298~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P3.4 [medium].** As shown in the figure below, a gas contained within a
piston–cylinder assembly, initially at a volume of $0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$, undergoes
a constant-pressure expansion at 2 bar to a final volume of $0.12~\mathrm{m^3}$,
while being slowly heated through the base. The increase in internal energy of
the gas is 0.25 kJ. The piston and cylinder walls are fabricated from
heat-resistant material, and the piston moves smoothly and slowly in the
cylinder (assume a quasi-equilibrium expansion). The local atmospheric pressure
is 1 bar. Evaluate the heat transfer magnitude through the base in kJ.

![](figures/img/ch3-p-piston-base.png){width=46%}

**(a)** 2.45 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 3.10 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 4.25 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 8.67

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**Given:** $P = 2$ bar, $V_1 = 0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$, $V_2 = 0.12~\mathrm{m^3}$,
$\Delta U = 0.25$ kJ; $Q = ?$

This is a quasi-equilibrium process, so $P_\text{ext} \approx P$ and we have:
$$
W = -\int P\,\mathrm{d}V
\;\xrightarrow{\ P\,=\,\text{const.}\ }\;
W = -P\left(V_2 - V_1\right)
= -2\times10^{5}~\mathrm{Pa}\times\left(0.02~\mathrm{m^3}\right)
= -4\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J}
$$

From the energy equation:
$$
Q + W = \Delta U
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
Q = \Delta U - W = 0.25~\mathrm{kJ} + 4~\mathrm{kJ}
= \boxed{4.25~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$

The atmospheric pressure is not needed: the gas pressure of 2 bar already
balances the atmosphere and the weight of the piston.
:::
:::

**P3.5 [medium].** A gas expands in a piston–cylinder assembly from
$p_1 = 8$ bar, $V_1 = 0.02~\mathrm{m^3}$ to $p_2 = 2$ bar in a
quasi-equilibrium process during which the relation between pressure and volume
is $pV^{1.2} = \text{constant}$. The mass of the gas is 0.25 kg. If the specific
internal energy of the gas decreases by 55 kJ/kg during the process, determine
the heat transfer in kJ. Kinetic and potential energy effects are negligible.

**(a)** 2.75 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 1.46 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 3.69 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 7.84

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**Given:** $m = 0.25$ kg, $P_1 = 8$ bar, $V_1 = 0.02~\mathrm{m^3}$,
$P_2 = 2$ bar, $PV^{1.2} = \text{constant}$, $\Delta u = -55$ kJ/kg.

As the process is quasi-equilibrium, $P_\text{ext} \approx P$, so we have:
$$
W = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,\mathrm{d}V
  = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2}\frac{\text{Const.}}{V^{1.2}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$
$$
W = \frac{\text{Const.}}{0.2}\left(V_2^{-0.2} - V_1^{-0.2}\right)
  = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{0.2}
\qquad (\text{Const.} = PV^{1.2})
$$

The volume at the final state is
$$
V_2 = \left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)^{1/1.2} V_1 = 4^{1/1.2}\times0.02 = 0.0635~\mathrm{m^3}
$$
thus
$$
W = \frac{\left(2\times10^{5}~\mathrm{Pa}\right)\left(0.0635~\mathrm{m^3}\right)
        - \left(8\times10^{5}~\mathrm{Pa}\right)\left(0.02~\mathrm{m^3}\right)}{0.2}
  = -16.5\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J} = -16.5~\mathrm{kJ}
$$

Now, to get the heat transfer, we use the energy equation (First Law):
$$
Q + W = \Delta U + \underbrace{\Delta KE}_{=\,0} + \underbrace{\Delta PE}_{=\,0}
$$

Solving for $Q$ and noting that $\Delta U = m\,\Delta u$:
$$
Q = m\,\Delta u - W
= \left(0.25~\mathrm{kg}\right)\left(-55~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg}}\right) + 16.5~\mathrm{kJ}
= \boxed{2.75~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

A positive heat transfer: energy is transferred **to** the gas by heat.
:::
:::

**P3.6 [medium].** A 250 litre rigid tank contains methane at 500 K,
1500 kPa. It is now cooled down to 300 K. Find the heat transfer in kJ.
(Assume ideal gas, $c_v = 1.736~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$ and
$R = 0.518~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** $-502.4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 367.8 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** $-487.6$
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 128

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
For a constant-volume process:
$$
Q = m\,c_v\,\Delta T \tag{I}
$$

We need to find the value of $m$. For an ideal gas:
$$
m = \frac{PV}{RT}
  = \frac{1500\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}\times250\times10^{-3}~\mathrm{m^3}}
         {518~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\times500~\mathrm{K}}
  = 1.448~\mathrm{kg} \tag{II}
$$

From (I) and (II):
$$
Q = 1.448~\mathrm{kg}\times1.736~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
    \times\left(300~\mathrm{K} - 500~\mathrm{K}\right)
  = \boxed{-502.7~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

Option (a), $-502.4$ kJ, is the same answer with the mass rounded down to
1.447 kg.
:::
:::

**P3.7 [medium].** A piston–cylinder contains air at 600 kPa, 290 K and a
volume of $0.01~\mathrm{m^3}$. In a reversible constant-pressure process, the
system does 18 kJ of work. Find the amount of heat transfer in kJ. (Assume ideal
gas, $R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$ and $c_P = 1000~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 62.7 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 35.6 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 128.9 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 26.9

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**Given:** $P_1 = P_2 = 600$ kPa, $T_1 = 290$ K, $V_1 = 0.01~\mathrm{m^3}$,
$W = -18$ kJ, $c_P = 1000~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$; $Q = ?$

First, we find the value of $V_2$ using the work relationship:
$$
W = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P_\text{ext}\,\mathrm{d}V
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{reversible process}\ }\;
W = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,\mathrm{d}V
\;\xrightarrow{\ P\,=\,\text{const.}\ }\;
W = -P\,\Delta V
$$
$$
-18\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J} = -600\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}\left(V_2 - 0.01~\mathrm{m^3}\right)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
V_2 = 0.04~\mathrm{m^3}
$$

From the ideal-gas equation, we can find the air mass:
$$
m = \frac{P_1V_1}{RT_1}
  = \frac{600\times10^{3}\times0.01~\mathrm{m^3}}{287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\times290~\mathrm{K}}
  = 0.0721~\mathrm{kg}
$$

We can also find $T_2$:
$$
PV = mRT \;\xrightarrow{\ P\,=\,\text{const.}\ }\;
\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}
\;\Rightarrow\;
T_2 = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)T_1
    = \left(\frac{0.04~\mathrm{m^3}}{0.01~\mathrm{m^3}}\right)290~\mathrm{K}
    = 1160~\mathrm{K}
$$

Now we can determine $Q$. For a constant-pressure process:
$$
Q_P = m\,c_P\,\Delta T
    = 0.0721~\mathrm{kg}\times1000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}\times870~\mathrm{K}
    = 6.27\times10^{4}~\mathrm{J} = \boxed{62.7~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P3.8 [medium].** A constant-pressure piston/cylinder contains 0.5 kg air at
300 K, 400 kPa. The system is heated to 1600 K. Find the magnitude of heat
transfer and its ratio to the work magnitude $|q/w|$. (Assume ideal gas and
$c_P = 1000~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 650 kJ, $c_v/R$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 350 kJ, 1 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 650 kJ, $(1 + c_v/R)$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 350 kJ, $c_v/R$

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
For a constant-pressure process:
$$
Q_P = m\,c_P\,\Delta T
    = 0.5~\mathrm{kg}\times1000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}\times1300~\mathrm{K}
    = 65\times10^{4}~\mathrm{J} = 650~\mathrm{kJ}
$$

Work in a reversible constant-pressure process, using $P\,\Delta V = mR\,\Delta T$
for an ideal gas:
$$
W = -P\,\Delta V
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{ideal gas}\ }\;
W = -mR\,\Delta T
\;\Rightarrow\;
|W| = mR\,\Delta T
$$

Therefore
$$
\left|\frac{Q}{W}\right| = \left|\frac{q}{w}\right|
= \frac{m\,c_P\,\Delta T}{m R\,\Delta T} = \frac{c_P}{R}
= \frac{R + c_v}{R} = 1 + \frac{c_v}{R}
$$

$$
\boxed{650~\mathrm{kJ},\;\; 1 + \frac{c_v}{R}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$
:::
:::

**P3.9 [medium].** A sealed chamber of $1~\mathrm{m^3}$ in volume is divided
into two halves by an impermeable diaphragm. Initially air at 20 °C and 1 bar is
contained in one half, and the other half is evacuated (i.e. total vacuum). The
diaphragm is removed, and the air is allowed to fill the whole chamber. What is
the final temperature (in Celsius) and pressure (bar) of the air? Assume ideal
gas behaviour and no heat exchange across the walls.

*Hint: you can first write the energy equation to find the change in internal
energy during this process. Then, you can try to relate this change to the
change in temperature. Once the final temperature is found, you should be able
to find the final pressure using the ideal-gas equation.*

**(a)** 10, 1 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 20, 0.5 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 20, 2
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 20, 0.5

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
State 1: 1 bar, 20 °C in one half, vacuum in the other. State 2: the whole
chamber, $P = ?$, $T = ?$

According to the energy equation, $Q + W = \Delta U$. Both $Q$ and $W$ are
zero. Note that the latter is zero because $P_\text{ext} = 0$ (free expansion).
Therefore:
$$
\Delta U = 0 \tag{I}
$$

For air as an ideal gas:
$$
\Delta U = m\,c_v\,\Delta T \tag{II}
$$

From (I) and (II):
$$
\Delta T = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = T_1 = 20~^\circ\mathrm{C}
$$

Also, $PV = mRT$, and both $m$ and $T$ do not change during the process, so:
$$
P_1V_1 = P_2V_2
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
P_2 = \left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)P_1 = 0.5\times1~\text{bar} = 0.5~\text{bar}
$$

$$
\boxed{20~^\circ\mathrm{C},\;\; 0.5~\text{bar}} \quad \text{(b)}
$$

(Options (b) and (d) are identical.)
:::
:::

**P3.10 [medium].** Air in a piston cylinder is at 1800 K, 7 MPa and expands in
a reversible polytropic process with $n = 1.5$ to a volume 8 times larger. Find
the heat transfer per unit mass in kJ/kg during this process. Assume air is an
ideal gas with $c_v = 0.717~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$ and
$R = 0.287~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.

**(a)** $-278.8$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 356.9 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 487.2
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** $-166.4$

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**Given:** $P_1 = 7$ MPa, $T_1 = 1800$ K, $v_1 = ?$; $v_2 = 8v_1$, $P_2 = ?$,
$T_2 = ?$

Use the ideal-gas equation to find $v_1$:
$$
v_1 = \frac{RT_1}{P_1}
    = \frac{287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\times1800~\mathrm{K}}{7\times10^{6}~\mathrm{Pa}}
    = 0.0738~\mathrm{m^3/kg}
$$

For a polytropic process with $n = 1.5$, $P_1v_1^{1.5} = P_2v_2^{1.5}$:
$$
P_2 = P_1\left(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^{n}
    = 7\times10^{6}~\mathrm{Pa}\times\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{1.5}
    = 3.09\times10^{5}~\mathrm{Pa}
$$

Now we can calculate the work per unit mass:
$$
w = \frac{P_2v_2 - P_1v_1}{n - 1}
  = \frac{3.09\times10^{5}\times8\times0.0738 - 7\times10^{6}\times0.0738}{1.5 - 1}
  = -6.679\times10^{5}~\mathrm{J/kg}
$$

To find the heat transfer, we can use the energy equation, with
$\Delta u = c_v\,\Delta T$ for an ideal gas and $T = Pv/R$:
$$
q + w = u_2 - u_1
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{ideal gas}\ }\;
q + w = c_v\left(T_2 - T_1\right) = \frac{c_v}{R}\left(P_2v_2 - P_1v_1\right)
$$
$$
q - 6.679\times10^{5}~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}
= \frac{717}{287}\left(3.09\times10^{5}\times8\times0.0738
  - 7\times10^{6}\times0.0738\right)\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}
= -8.343\times10^{5}~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}
$$
$$
q = -1.664\times10^{5}~\mathrm{J/kg} = \boxed{-166.4~\mathrm{kJ/kg}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
:::
:::

**P3.11 [medium].** A piston cylinder contains 0.1 kg air at 300 K and
100 kPa. The air is now slowly compressed in a reversible isothermal process to
a final pressure of 250 kPa. Show the process in a $PV$ diagram and find the
heat transfer in kJ in the process. (Air is an ideal gas with
$R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** $-7.89$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 3.69 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** $-2.6$
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 7.89

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
In an isothermal process (i.e. a polytropic process with $n = 1$) for an ideal
gas, the pressure rises along $PV = mRT = \text{const}$ as the volume falls,
from $V_1 = mRT/P_1 = 0.086~\mathrm{m^3}$ to
$V_2 = mRT/P_2 = 0.034~\mathrm{m^3}$:

![](figures/out/ch3-p-isothermal-sol.svg){width=52%}

The work is
$$
W = -P_1V_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{ideal gas: } P_1V_1\,=\,mRT\ }\;
W = -mRT\ln\!\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) \tag{I}
$$

For the isothermal process, $P_1V_1 = mRT$ and $P_2V_2 = mRT$, so
$$
\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{P_1}{P_2} \tag{II}
$$

From (I) and (II):
$$
W = -mRT_1\ln\!\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)
  = -0.1~\mathrm{kg}\times287~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}\times300~\mathrm{K}
    \times\ln\!\left(\frac{100~\mathrm{kPa}}{250~\mathrm{kPa}}\right)
  = 7.89\times10^{3}~\mathrm{J}
$$

From the energy equation for an ideal gas, with $\Delta T = 0$ ($T$ constant):
$$
Q + W = \Delta U = m\,c_v\,\underbrace{\Delta T}_{=\,0}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
Q = -W = \boxed{-7.89~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::
